You know "I can see Russia from my house." Palin never said it in 2008. But from this Alaskan island, you really can. Is it 2.4 miles away?
NASA says 2.4. National Geographic says 1.8. The Park Service says 2.7. And across that water, it's already tomorrow.
So, three questions. Who actually said that line? How far away is Russia, really? And why couldn't anyone cross for forty years?
First, the line. Everyone remembers Sarah Palin saying it.
We pulled the transcript.
On September 11, 2008, ABC's Charlie Gibson asked Palin what insight Alaska's closeness to Russia gave her.
Her answer, in the transcript from the American Presidency Project: "They're our next door neighbors. And you can actually see Russia from land here in Alaska."
No house.
Two days later, on the season premiere of Saturday Night Live, Tina Fey played Palin. And Fey's Palin said: "And I can see Russia from my house."
Snopes calls it a line that originated with an SNL spoof. According to Wikipedia, it was written by an SNL producer, Mike Shoemaker.
So the famous quote isn't hers. But her actual claim is a different question. Can you actually see Russia from land in Alaska?
To answer that, we need a map.
Here's Alaska. Here's Russia. Between them, the Bering Strait.
At its narrowest, NASA says about 82 kilometers, or 51 miles, of water separate Cape Prince of Wales in Alaska from Cape Dezhnev in Russia.
The Park Service rounds it to about 55 miles.
Either way, too far to see a house.
But zoom in. Right in the middle of the strait, there are two islands.
The small one is Little Diomede. It belongs to the United States.
The big one is Big Diomede. It belongs to Russia.
And this is where the numbers start to disagree.
NASA's Earth Observatory, measuring from Landsat satellite images: 3.8 kilometers. 2.4 miles.
Slate, in 2008: a little less than two and a half miles.
The Park Service's Alaska page: about 2.5 miles.
Another Park Service page: 2.7 miles.
National Geographic's main text says about two miles. Its photo caption says 1.8.
Six sources. Five different numbers.
So we measured it ourselves.
Using Natural Earth map data, the closest points of the two islands come out about 3.9 kilometers apart. About 2.45 miles.
That's a rough map, built for the whole world, not for two small islands. But it lands right next to NASA's number.
So the best answer is about 2.4 miles. The 1.8 looks like the odd one out. The 2.7 too. We couldn't find what it was measuring.
That's closer than a lot of people's commute.
Now, can you see across?
According to NASA, the village on Little Diomede sits on the island's western side. Big Diomede, and even the Russian mainland, are visible from the homes.
Slate adds a catch. The islands are often wrapped in fog. But on a clear day, you can definitely see one from the other.
So Palin's line checks out. From land in Alaska, on a clear day, you can see Russia.
But the strangest thing about this view isn't the distance. It's the date.
Part two. Yesterday Island and Tomorrow Island.
Where does the border actually run?
It was drawn in 1867, when the United States bought Alaska from Russia for 7.2 million dollars.
Here's the treaty, from the State Department's historical archive.
The western limit, it says, passes through a point in the Bering Strait, on the meridian which passes midway between the island of Krusenstern, and the island of Ratmanoff.
Krusenstern is Little Diomede. Ratmanoff is Big Diomede.
So the line runs straight down the water between them.
And the International Date Line follows that border here.
That's why Little Diomede got the nickname Yesterday Island, and Big Diomede, Tomorrow Island.
NASA even quoted a reader: "When you look at the Big Diomede Island, you're looking into the future!"
But how far into the future?
Snopes and Wikipedia say 21 hours. National Geographic says 23.
So we checked the clocks.
Little Diomede runs on Alaska time. In winter, that's nine hours behind UTC. Big Diomede runs on Russia's Anadyr time, twelve hours ahead.
That's 21 hours. In summer, Alaska moves its clocks forward, so it's 20.
So at noon on a Monday in January on Little Diomede, it's already 9 a.m. on Tuesday across the water.
National Geographic's 23 doesn't match the clocks.
So you can see Russia. You can see tomorrow. But for most of the last century, you couldn't go there.
Part three. The Ice Curtain.
For a long time, the line between the islands barely mattered.
According to National Geographic, the Iñupiat on both islands were deeply connected. They married across the strait and shared the same customs.
In winter, the water froze into an ice bridge, and people walked between the islands.
One Little Diomede tribal coordinator told the magazine her grandfather used to cross back and forth all the time.
Then came the Cold War. And the line on the treaty map suddenly mattered.
In 1948, National Geographic reports, the Soviet government forcibly evacuated Big Diomede. Its people were moved to the mainland, and the island was turned into a military base.
The water between the islands got a new name: the Ice Curtain.
Families were split by two and a half miles of water.
For almost forty years, that's how it stayed. So what finally cracked it?
Then, a swimmer.
In 1976, according to the Park Service, an American swimmer named Lynne Cox came up with an idea: swim from Little Diomede to Big Diomede.
It took her eleven years to get permission. Would the Soviets even let her land?
In 1987, she flew to Little Diomede. Thirty hours before the swim, there was still no word from the Soviet side.
Permission finally came 24 hours before, from Mikhail Gorbachev.
On August 7, 1987, she stepped into 38 degree water.
She later said her fingers turned grey, like the hands of a cadaver.
Two hours and five minutes later, she reached Big Diomede. She reached out, and two Russians in military uniform grabbed her.
Later that year, when Gorbachev came to Washington to sign a nuclear weapons treaty, he and Ronald Reagan raised a glass to her.
Gorbachev said she proved by her courage how close to each other our peoples live.
A year later, in June 1988, a Friendship Flight carried officials, reporters, and Alaska Natives from Nome to Provideniya in Russia.
The Park Service says it was the first direct flight from Alaska to Russia in over forty years.
So, was the curtain gone for good?
Not quite.
Part four. Two miles, the long way.
When National Geographic visited Little Diomede, five Russians who used to live on Big Diomede were coming to see their relatives.
The trip across the water is about two miles.
They couldn't take it.
Instead, they flew from Russia to Nome, then on to the Alaskan town of Wales, then took a helicopter out to the island.
Bad weather held them up. They landed five days behind schedule. Two miles of water. Five days late.
And the ice that once connected the islands is changing too.
Little Diomede used to carve a winter runway into the sea ice for planes. National Geographic says it no longer has one, because the ice has grown too thin.
Now the main link to the mainland is an occasional helicopter.
So one last check. What about the mainland? Can you see Russia from there?
Slate asked the station chief at the Tin City radar site, on Cape Prince of Wales, the westernmost tip of mainland North America.
His answer: for roughly half the year, you can see Siberian mountain ranges from the highest part of the site.
Not from a house. From a radar station on a mountain.
So, the check.
Claim one: Sarah Palin said, "I can see Russia from my house."
False. That was Tina Fey on Saturday Night Live.
Claim two: you can see Russia from land in Alaska.
True. From Little Diomede, on a clear day, you can see Big Diomede. And from the top of Cape Prince of Wales, Siberia's mountains for part of the year.
Claim three: Russia is 2.4 miles from Alaska.
True. NASA's number holds up. The 1.8 doesn't.
And one bonus. Across that water, it really is tomorrow. 21 hours of tomorrow in winter.
Two and a half miles. Almost a whole day. And for forty years, a wall made of ice.
Would you live on Yesterday Island, looking at tomorrow every morning? Tell me in the comments.
